slides.title: Collecting the specimen
bullets: One fresh voided specimen is enough for a routine test: it is collected in a container that is convenient for the patient, wide-mouthed, clean, dry and intact, with no traces of disinfectant.
The urine must contain no vaginal discharge or menstrual blood; before collection the external genitalia are washed from front to back.
The midstream part of the first morning urine is the most concentrated: it is very suitable for protein, nitrites, microscopy, specific gravity and the pregnancy test.
A daytime midstream specimen is suitable for chemical tests and for culture, but not for measuring specific gravity.
Explain to the patient how to collect a midstream sample: first void a little into the toilet, then collect the rest in a clean dry container.

slides.title: Collecting the specimen
bullets: For bacteriological tests only a sterile container is used; the urine is submitted before antibacterial treatment starts, and the first portion goes into the toilet.

slides.title: Storage and delay errors
bullets: Collected urine should be tested within one hour.
If the test is delayed, bacteria multiply and use up glucose: the glucose result is wrong, the pH shifts to alkaline, red cells lyse and casts break down.
Until testing begins, specimens are kept in a refrigerator.
Appearance and colour are judged in the light and recorded; turbidity may come from many epithelial cells in a badly collected sample, red cells, white cells, bacteria or salts.

slides.title: Volume, colour and clarity
bullets: 1. Give each specimen a serial number; inspect it in the light and record its appearance and colour.
2. Normal urine is straw-yellow and, when fresh, clear; the colour is altered by urochromes, urobilin and other pigments, as well as by food, drugs and vitamins.
3. To measure the volume pour the urine gently into a measuring cylinder and record the meniscus mark.
4. The daily volume depends on fluid intake, type of diet, climate and sweating.
5. In the Kurbonova book polyuria is more than 2000 mL a day, oliguria less than 500 mL and anuria 100 mL or less.

slides.title: Specific gravity
bullets: 1. Specific gravity shows the ability of the kidneys to concentrate or dilute urine.
2. Methods: a urinometer, a refractometer or reagent test strips.
3. Urinometer: pour the uncentrifuged midstream morning specimen into a measuring cylinder, lower the urinometer gently and let go — it must float without touching the bottom or the walls.
4. Read the scale at the lower point of the urine meniscus at eye level.
5. Check a new urinometer in distilled water before use: it must read 1.000; if it does not, subtract the difference from later results.
6. Dip the test strip into the urine for 3–5 seconds and read the result after 30 seconds.

slides.title: Safety
bullets: Specimen containers must have lids; the specimen must not spill out.
Wear single-use gloves when handling specimens; after work wash the hands with soap or wipe them with an alcohol solution.
Specimens are kept in a spill-proof container while being processed, stored and transported.

Pour leftover urine carefully, without splashing, into the toilet of the washing room; put containers and instruments into a disinfectant solution (concentration and time according to the regulation in force).
